# Rethinking backward-looking moral responsibility as care robots move toward superintelligence

- Perspective
- Open access
- Published: 26 February 2026

- Mario Kropf ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-0645-3276 1 

## Abstract

The use of AI-based care robots raises numerous questions, including the attribution of responsibility. Although there is a wealth of work on the concept of responsibility in relation to AI-based systems, this article takes a new approach. It focuses on backward-looking moral responsibility for bad outcomes and super-intelligent care robots. The starting point is the presentation of realistic scenarios in which current care robots contribute to responsibility gaps. A distinction is made between forward-looking and backward-looking moral responsibility, with a focus on backward-looking moral responsibility for bad outcomes. Using hypothetical scenarios such as careful programmer, unlucky nurse, and robot mistake, it is shown that current robots do not fulfill central conditions (control, knowledge, intention) for moral responsibility. In such scenarios, however, the attribution of moral responsibility to human actors has to be seen as a burden. Afterward, super-intelligent care robots are examined. Such machines could not only fill responsibility gaps, but also actively contribute to the avoidance of bad outcomes. Approaches to collective or extended responsibility are discussed. Finally, it is argued that moral responsibility concerning super-intelligent care robots is not only possible but could be necessary in order to address moral responsibility adequately.

## 1 Introduction

AI systems are increasingly being assigned to areas where people are vulnerable and dependent on support, such as in the care sector. Care robots can encourage people, monitor health data, enable new interactions, or support staff [66, 97]. Such machines act, but they are not autonomous. But what happens when these AI systems become better (more autonomous)? And what are the consequences of super-intelligent care robots? Although authors [2, 9, 33, 51] have already addressed similar questions, using care robots is new. This article deals with super-intelligent care robots and backward-looking moral responsibility for bad outcomes. In a first step, care robots are considered. The second step discusses backward-looking moral responsibility for bad outcomes and related to these machines. The third step involves making plausible assumptions about super-intelligent care robots. It is shown that (1) backward-looking moral responsibility in AI-supported care contexts imposes a particular burden, (2) that current robots structurally create responsibility gaps, thereby unjustifiably imposing this burden on humans, and (3) that super-intelligent care robots—under plausible assumptions—could fill these gaps and thus become suitable bearers of backward-looking moral responsibility.

A care robot can be conceived as a physically embodied artificial actor that is capable of providing supportive care to people due to its technical skills [49]. In this context, human–machine interaction can lead to people in need of care perceiving the robots as social entities. Footnote 1 Verbal and nonverbal interaction is possible, and care robots are usually developed specifically for vulnerable groups such as elderly people, children with special needs, or people with dementia [46, 60, 79]. In the following, I will discuss socially assistive robots (SARs), which sets the stage for considerations regarding super-intelligent care robots. SARs not only perform assistance functions but also make a social contribution. They assist with communication and mobility, deliver medication, monitor health conditions, act as moderators, and are currently the most advanced models in healthcare [48, 72, 89]. Examples include Pepper, the Kompaï robot and NAO, which have a humanoid design. PR2, Lio, and Care-O-bot, in contrast, have a non-humanoid design. MARIO and RobAlz are being developed specifically for certain groups [53, 73]. But why these machines? SARs are considered because, firstly, it can be assumed that these machines and more advanced models will continue to play an important role in care facilities in the future [65, 92]. Secondly, because of the nature of care itself and the fact that technical forms of support are (and will be) increasingly considered. And thirdly, because human–robot interaction offers certain possibilities that do not arise in purely human interactions. The word “care” in care robot does not mean that these machines can completely take over human care. Expecting NAO to lift a person out of bed, Pepper to treat wounds, or Lio to be responsible for a person’s personal hygiene is neither in line with the capabilities of current machines nor their intended area of application.

However, it can be assumed that super-intelligent robots have advantages over non-physically embodied super-intelligent systems because they act in the world [3, 32, 54]. Although work [36, 62, 63, 84] has already been done on different forms of responsibility relating to AI-based robots, this article takes a new approach by focussing on moral responsibility for bad outcomes and super-intelligent care robots. SARs offer certain advantages over other AI-based systems or robots with fewer technical capabilities. They can (1) move semi-autonomously in a predefined environment, which the robot seal Paro, for example, cannot do. They have (2) communicative abilities, which facilitates exchange and interaction with humans. And it seems (3) plausible that the development of super-intelligent care robots will be based on what advanced SARs can do, rather than taking a completely different path. If the use of these machines is also intended to contribute to learning from the feedback of people being cared for, taking their wishes and suggestions seriously, and thus adapting future models accordingly, then SARs are an important basis for (conceivable) super-intelligent robots. A complete disregard of current experience seems neither plausible nor justifiable. Such a strategy would be implausible because it can be assumed that even super-intelligent robots should interact and coexist with humans in an adequate manner. Not considering the perspective of people in need of care—and other individuals—in the further development of these machines would, in a sense, run counter to one’s own preferences, because all humans can end up in need of care and dependent on AI. Furthermore, current perspectives and attitudes toward AI-based robots are a good indication of what humans will expect from (super-intelligent) robots in the future. Such a strategy would be difficult to justify because it would mean that the interests, needs, and fears of people receiving care would not be given much relevance. At the same time, it contradicts the purpose of care robots, which are assigned to people who need support and are vulnerable—in other words, developed specifically for them.

## 2 Moral responsibility for bad outcomes and AI based care robots

The term moral responsibility is associated with a variety of ideas, such as causality, freedom, intentionality, and normativity, prospective and retrospective forms, or subjective and collective responsibility. As already indicated, this article focuses on backward-looking moral responsibility for bad outcomes. What does that mean? Based on the considerations of Watson, Smith and Shoemaker, a distinction is usually made between (1) attributability, (2) answerability, and (3) accountability [74, 78, 91]. While (1) attributability involves assessing a person’s character (or deep self) on the basis of a specific action, (2) answerability involves assessing a person’s evaluative judgment. And (3) accountability entails an assessment of the actor based on the original evaluation of an action. This can entail blame if and then because the interests of others were not sufficiently considered. The distinction between (1) and (3) roughly corresponds to what Zimmerman means by thin and thick blame [96]. For example, one might be upset (thin blame) with a friend who forgets one’s birthday. However, if the friend says they are sorry, one might refrain from further accusations (thick blame), or not. Such assessments or reactions can be reconciled with Strawson’s reactive attitudes, which have been widely discussed and shape our practice of moral responsibility [82]. This practice already includes AI-based care robots and, possibly in the future, super-intelligent versions of them. In short, what I mean by moral responsibility in this article is accountability (thick blame Footnote 2) in a backward-looking sense.

The following starting point will be taken for the rest of this article: The degree of moral responsibility of an agent (A) for an action Footnote 3 (X) and associated bad outcomes (O) is based on facts about A, X, O, and the relationships between them [44, 45]. However, A must be a moral agent, because moral responsibility implies that A is aware of the moral relevance of this responsibility [16, 62]. Bad outcomes are understood to be something bad that reasonably qualifies as such. While rain is also a bad outcome if A1 wants to play tennis, it is more clearly a bad outcome if A2 is killed by lightning, regardless of whether A2 wanted to play tennis or not. This personal focus stems from the fact that bad outcomes involve more complex issues than positive actions, which might result in praise. When AI-based systems act, for example, it has been suggested that moral responsibility should be taken on by individual (human) actors or a group (of humans) in order to prevent the frequently discussed responsibility gaps [15, 55, 64]. However, what I believe is often neglected or at least not analyzed in sufficient detail is the moral relevance of this responsibility gap. Footnote 4 It is not uncommon to get the impression that causal connections between A, X and O are sufficient to close responsibility gaps. This may be true for causal responsibility, but not for moral responsibility, as will be made clear in the following passages. Let’s consider the example careful programmer:

> A programmer (P1) revises NAO’s control algorithms because the robot repeatedly failed to respond adequately to user commands. The aim of the adjustment is to ensure that commands from people receiving care are implemented more reliably. An ethically legitimate exception is the prevention of harm to oneself or others. P1 takes sufficient time for the adapted programming, considers possible negative consequences, and ensures that the machine’s decision-making logic remains compatible with bioethical principles. In short, P1 acts conscientiously and carefully, without malicious intent.

The present example corresponds to a forward-looking moral responsibility of P1, which, although seemingly contrary to the concern of this article, is crucial for the comprehensibility of the position taken here, as the following passages show. Following Nelkin, Fischer, and Ravizza, moral responsibility refers to a person acting in accordance with certain (moral) reasons [23, 26, 61]—or, in other words, being able to follow a reasons responsive mechanism. A distinction is made between (1) recognizing moral reasons and (2) following them [25, 29, 39]. In the scenario described, it can be argued that P1 not only (1) recognized that NAO should follow the instructions of people receiving care—with plausible exceptions—and that, for example, the avoidance of harm should be integrated into the machine’s code as a guideline, but that P1 was also (2) motivated to carry out the corresponding actions.
